content: Gestational hypertension, also known as pregnancy-induced hypertension (PIH), is defined as a systolic blood pressure (SBP) greater than 140 mmHg and/or a diastolic blood pressure (DBP) greater than 90 mmHg on at least two separate occasions, measured at least six hours apart, after the 20th week of gestation in women who were normotensive prior to pregnancy and before 20 weeks of gestation. The blood pressure readings used to confirm the diagnosis should not be more than seven days apart. Gestational hypertension is classified as severe if there is a sustained elevation in systolic blood pressure to at least 160 mmHg and/or diastolic blood pressure to at least 110 mmHg for a minimum of six hours. This condition is one of the most common medical disorders affecting pregnancy. The treatment of gestational hypertension depends on several factors, including the blood pressure levels, gestational age, presence of symptoms, and associated risk factors. The exact cause of gestational hypertension remains unknown. If left untreated, severe gestational hypertension can lead to life-threatening complications, including seizures (eclampsia) and even death of the mother and fetus. Due to these risks, early delivery of the baby, before full-term pregnancy, may be necessary. Certain conditions increase the risk of developing gestational hypertension, including: A history of hypertension Kidney disease Diabetes Hypertension during a previous pregnancy Maternal age younger than 20 or older than 40 Multiple gestations (e.g., twins, triplets) African-American race Theories regarding the pathogenesis of gestational hypertension include: Insufficient blood flow to the uterus or abnormal placental implantation Damage to the blood vessels Immune system dysfunction Genetic factors Platelet activation Hyperlipidemia and insulin resistance Management of gestational hypertension remains a topic of debate, as does the classification of its severity. Delaying the interruption of pregnancy in cases of severe gestational hypertension may result in the progression to preeclampsia, which can lead to placental insufficiency, maternal organ dysfunction, and increased risks of maternal and perinatal mortality. The goals of management are to minimize pregnancy-related complications, avoid unnecessary prematurity, and optimize maternal and infant survival. Recommended actions (Dos) for pregnant women with gestational hypertension include: Regular visits to a healthcare provider throughout the pregnancy. Adherence to prescribed blood pressure medications. Ensuring that the healthcare provider prescribes the safest medication at the most appropriate dose. Staying physically active and following the healthcare provider's recommendations for physical activity. Maintaining a healthy diet and consulting a nutritionist if additional guidance is needed. Consulting the healthcare provider before taking any over-the-counter medications. Actions to avoid (Don'ts) for pregnant women with gestational hypertension include: Strength training and pure isometric exercises, such as weightlifting and aerobic exercise, as these can acutely elevate blood pressure to dangerous levels and increase the risk of adverse events like stroke. Restricting sodium intake during pregnancy, as there is no evidence to suggest that this prevents preeclampsia. Consuming alcohol, recreational drugs, or smoking.
